title: Component Dating and Processing: Washed, Deglycerolized, Irradiated, Albumin
summary: Apply the US federal dating periods for red cells, platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate, explain that washing or opening a bag cuts red-cell dating to 24 hours, and know the heat treatment required for albumin.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 41 Hits 19 and 20 with the full 21 CFR 610.53 dating table as context. Checked against 21 CFR 610.53, 21 CFR 640.81 and Cugno 2015. US federal rules only; Philippine rules were not checked. Not taught: granulocytes “must be ABO-compatible” (Hit 12) and room-temperature storage, ISBT 128 DIN details (Hit 15), and platelet swirling (Hit 21) — not in the sources read.

objectives: State US dating periods for red cells by preservative and processing, platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate.
Apply the open-system, closed-deglycerolization and irradiation dating rules to a unit.
Describe the heat treatment required for albumin.

scenes.title: Same red cells, four different expiry dates
scenes.altText: A shelf with four bags from the same donation-type: an AS-1 red cell unit (day 10 of 42), the same unit after washing in an open system, a deglycerolized unit processed in a closed system with additive, and an irradiated unit. A vial of 5% albumin sits beside them. Question token: “When does each expire — and what processing does albumin need?” The cartoon scientist checks labels.

cues.text: Four red-cell bags sit on the shelf: a standard additive-solution unit, the same kind of unit after washing in an open system, a closed-system deglycerolized unit, and an irradiated unit.
Beside them is a vial of 5 percent albumin, made from pooled plasma.
Processing changes the expiry date, and albumin has its own required processing. Which date goes on each label?

scenes.title: The federal dating table
scenes.altText: A table card (21 CFR 610.53, US): Red Blood Cells, 1–6 °C — CPD 21 days, CPDA-1 35 days, additive solutions 42 days from collection; open system (deglycerolized, washed) 24 hours after entering the bag; deglycerolized in a closed system with additive 14 days; irradiated 28 days from irradiation or original dating, whichever is shorter; frozen at −65 °C or colder 10 years. Platelets 20–24 °C: 5 days (unless the storage system’s FDA-cleared instructions say otherwise). Fresh frozen plasma −18 °C or colder: 1 year. Cryoprecipitated AHF −18 °C or colder: 1 year.

cues.text: In the United States, 21 CFR 610.53 sets dating periods. Red cells at 1 to 6 degrees last 21 days in CPD, 35 in CPDA-1, and 42 in additive solutions.
Open the system, for washing or deglycerolizing, and the red cells expire 24 hours after the bag is entered.
Deglycerolized red cells processed in a closed system with additive solution keep 14 days. Irradiated red cells expire 28 days after irradiation or at the original date, whichever comes first.
Frozen red cells at minus 65 or colder keep 10 years. Platelets at 20 to 24 degrees keep 5 days, unless the FDA-cleared storage system allows otherwise.
Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate, at minus 18 or colder, keep one year.

lines: CPD 21 d · CPDA-1 35 d · AS 42 d

scenes.title: Processing resets the clock
scenes.altText: A timeline for one additive-solution red-cell unit (schematic). Collected: 42-day dating. Washed in an open system: the clock resets to 24 hours after the bag is entered. Deglycerolized in a closed system with additive solution: 14 days after the bag is entered. Irradiated on day 30: expires on day 42 (original date), because 28 days from irradiation would be later. Irradiated on day 5: expires on day 33 (28 days after irradiation). A granulocyte card: current standards limit storage to 24 hours (one review: after 2 days at 4 °C only 2–7% remain viable).

cues.text: Processing resets the clock. Take one additive-solution unit: on collection it has 42 days.
Wash it in an open system and it now expires 24 hours after the bag was entered, regardless of the original date.
Deglycerolize it in a closed system with additive solution, and it keeps 14 days after the bag is entered.
Irradiate it on day 30 and it still expires on day 42, because the original date comes first. Irradiate it on day 5 and it expires on day 33, 28 days later.
Granulocytes are the shortest-lived product: current standards limit storage to 24 hours, and after two days in the cold only a few percent remain viable.

scenes.title: Albumin: made safe by heat
scenes.altText: An albumin manufacturing card (21 CFR 640.81): final containers heated continuously for 10–11 hours at 60 ± 0.5 °C, starting within 24 hours of filling; sodium caprylate (± acetyltryptophanate) stabilizer present; then incubated at 20–35 °C for at least 14 days and inspected — turbid containers are not issued. Back to the hook: AS unit 42 days from collection; washed (open) 24 h; closed deglycerolized 14 d; irradiated 28 d or original, whichever is shorter.

cues.text: Albumin is made from pooled plasma. The federal rule requires the final containers to be heated continuously for 10 to 11 hours at 60 degrees.
A stabilizer, sodium caprylate, must be present. Afterwards, every container is incubated for at least 14 days and inspected; any turbid container is withheld.
Heating starts within 24 hours of filling. The rule sets the time and temperature precisely: not less than 10 hours and not more than 11.
Back to the shelf: the additive-solution unit keeps 42 days from collection; the washed open-system unit, 24 hours.
The closed-system deglycerolized unit, 14 days; the irradiated unit, 28 days or its original date, whichever is shorter.

props.label: Heating starts within 24 h of filling

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Washed red cells keep the original expiry” (✓ open system → 24 hours after entering the bag); “Irradiated units always get 28 more days” (✓ 28 days or original dating, whichever is shorter); “Frozen red cells keep 1 year” (✓ 10 years at −65 °C or colder).

cues.text: Trap one: washed red cells keep their original expiry. Washing opens the system, so they expire 24 hours after the bag is entered.
Trap two: irradiation gives a unit 28 more days. It is 28 days from irradiation or the original date, whichever is shorter.
Trap three: frozen red cells keep one year. At minus 65 degrees or colder they keep 10 years; one year is the plasma and cryoprecipitate rule.

scenes.title: Open = one day
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Open is one day; closed deglycerolized is two weeks; irradiation is four weeks — never longer than the original.” Tokens 24 h / 14 d / 28 d. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: open is one day; closed deglycerolized is two weeks; irradiation is four weeks, but never longer than the original date.
Where it breaks: FDA-cleared storage systems can specify other dating; rules outside the US differ; and local policies can be stricter.

explanation.what: Plain language: every blood product has a shelf life, and processing a unit (washing, deglycerolizing, irradiating) changes it; albumin must be heat-treated. Scientific terms: dating period, open vs closed system, deglycerolization, additive solution (AS), irradiation, Albumin (Human), pasteurization, sodium caprylate.
explanation.why: Federal dating periods depend on the anticoagulant/preservative, storage temperature and whether the system has been opened or the unit irradiated. Albumin is a plasma-derived product; its processing rule requires heat treatment of the final containers with a stabilizer present.
explanation.measure: 21 CFR 610.53: RBC CPD 21 d, CPDA-1 35 d, AS 42 d; open system 24 h; closed deglycerolized with AS 14 d; irradiated 28 d or original, shorter; frozen ≤ −65 °C 10 y; platelets 20–24 °C 5 d (or per FDA-cleared system); FFP and cryo ≤ −18 °C 1 y. 21 CFR 640.81: albumin final containers 60 ± 0.5 °C for 10–11 h, then ≥ 14-day incubation at 20–35 °C. Granulocyte storage limited to 24 h.
explanation.differs: Open vs closed processing; irradiated (28 d or original, shorter) vs non-irradiated (original); frozen RBC (10 y) vs frozen plasma and cryo (1 y).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: washed RBC expiry, irradiated dating rule, frozen RBC 10 years, platelet 5 days, FFP/cryo 1 year, and albumin heat treatment.

questions.stem: An additive-solution red cell unit collected 10 days ago is washed in an open system at 09:00 today. When does it expire?

options.text: 09:00 tomorrow (24 hours after entering the bag)
options.rationale: Correct. Open-system processing limits red cells to 24 hours after the bag is entered.
Incorrect. The original dating no longer applies once the system is opened.
Incorrect. 14 days applies to closed-system deglycerolized units with additive solution.
Incorrect. 28 days is the irradiation rule.

questions.stem: An AS red cell unit collected 30 days ago is irradiated today. What is its new expiration?

options.text: Day 42 from collection (12 days from now) — the original date is shorter than 28 days
options.rationale: Correct. Irradiated RBCs expire 28 days after irradiation or at the original date, whichever is shorter.
Incorrect. That would exceed the original 42-day dating.
Incorrect. Irradiation does not open the system.
Incorrect. 35 days applies to CPDA-1, not additive solution.

questions.stem: Which processing step does 21 CFR 640.81 require for the final containers of Albumin (Human)?

options.text: Heating final containers at 60 °C for 10–11 hours
options.rationale: Correct. The rule requires continuous heating at 60 ± 0.5 °C for 10–11 hours with a stabilizer present.
Incorrect. Irradiation is used for cellular components to prevent TA-GVHD.
Incorrect. Leukoreduction is not part of the albumin processing rule.
Incorrect. The rule specifies heating of the final containers, not freezing.
